```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(lme4))

# Formatting helpers for numbers printed in the text.
f <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 0) {
  paste(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "per cent")
}
nw <- function(n) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
             "nine", "ten")
  if (n >= 1 && n <= 10 && n == round(n)) words[n] else
    formatC(n, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
}
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) <= 1) return(x)
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
```

# Summary {.unnumbered}

theoryforge reads a scientific theory written as a structured file and
computes from it what the stated causal graph implies, how completely the file
states what its checklist asks for and how a later version of the file compares
with an earlier one. Its computations on a given file are correct. What has not
been studied is everything that happens before and after the file: whether
different researchers encode the same verbal theory into files that give the
same results, whether the checklist score and the item statuses agree with
expert judgements of how completely and how testably a theory is specified,
whether the verdicts of `appraise_amendment()` agree with expert appraisals of
the same amendments, and whether readers take the outputs to mean what they
say.

This protocol describes three studies that would decide what can be claimed.
Study 1 measures how reliably trained coders encode published verbal theories,
from the elements of the file to the derived implications and the checklist
score, and compares that agreement with human and agent baselines. Study 2
compares the checklist and the appraisal with blind expert ratings and tests
whether known groups of corroborated, refuted and pseudoscientific theories
differ as they should. Study 3 is a randomised reader study that compares the
rate at which researchers and editors misread the score, the gate, the dossier
and the appraisal in the wording of version 0.7.0 and of version 0.8.0. A last
section outlines a later cliometric study of predictive validity. Every number
in this document is computed by the R code it contains, from inputs stated in
that code or read from the repository, so that a change of assumption changes
every number that depends on it.

# Background {#sec-background}

## What the package computes and what it does not

```{r}
#| label: inputs-external
# Values reported by published sources, as stated in the place named.
external <- list(
  # Bornmann, Mutz and Daniel (2010), abstract and Table 1: mean reliability
  # between reviewers of the same manuscript on the intraclass correlation
  # scale (random-effects model; product-moment correlations were squared to
  # that scale), and mean Cohen's kappa.
  reviewer_icc = 0.34, reviewer_kappa = 0.17,
  # Hoekstra et al. (2014), abstract: researchers and students endorsed, on
  # average, more than three of six false statements about a confidence
  # interval.
  false_endorsed = 3, false_items = 6,
  # Hale et al. (2020), abstract: theories represented and sent to authors or
  # experts for feedback, and those finalised only after changes to their
  # constructs, relations or both.
  hale_theories = 71, hale_changed = 36,
  # Juni et al. (1999), abstract: quality scales used to identify
  # high-quality trials in one meta-analysis.
  juni_scales = 25
)
```

theoryforge takes as input a file that lists a theory's constructs,
propositions, predictions, phenomena, rivals, assumptions and test outcomes.
From the file it derives the conditional independencies and the signs of
effects that the causal graph of the propositions implies, scores the file
against a checklist, compares the theory with rivals and appraises an amended
version against an earlier one by fixed rules that borrow the terms of
@lakatos1970. Checks made before the 0.8.0 release found the deductive
computations correct: they agree with independent implementations on every
file examined. The same checks found three gaps that no computation on a file
can close.

The first gap is encoding. A verbal theory does not determine its file. In an
encoding pilot (@sec-pilot), encoders given the same source texts produced
files that agreed on the plain statements of a theory and differed on what the
texts leave open, and the derived implications followed the files.
@hale2020 report a similar difficulty for a related representation: of
`r external$hale_theories` behaviour change theories represented as
construct-relationship triples, `r external$hale_changed` were finalised only
after changes to their constructs, their relations or both, following feedback
from the theories' authors or other experts. Whatever the package derives is
therefore a property of an encoding. Whether it is also a property of the
theory depends on how much encodings agree, which is unknown for human
encoders.

The second gap is the checklist score. The checklist reads whether fields are
filled in, how predictions are labelled and whether stated claims agree with
the causal graph. Version 0.8.0 calls the result the checklist score and
states that it describes how completely the file states what the checklist
asks for, that no study has established what difference between two scores is
meaningful and that the score does not show that the theory is true or well
reasoned. That statement describes the file correctly. It leaves open whether
the score, or the item statuses behind it, track what methodologists mean by a
completely and testably specified theory. Summary quality scores have a poor
record elsewhere: when @juni1999 used `r external$juni_scales` quality scales
to identify the high-quality trials in one meta-analysis, some scales showed an
effect only in the high-quality trials and others only in the low-quality ones,
and the summary scores were not significantly associated with the estimated
treatment effects. Validity
concerns the inferences drawn from scores, and @messick1995 distinguishes
content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external and consequential
aspects of the evidence for them. For this score, none has been examined.

The third gap is the appraisal. `appraise_amendment()` labels an amendment
progressive, degenerating or neutral by rules applied to what the two files
declare. The rules are explicit and reproducible, but their agreement with the
appraisals that researchers or historians would make of the same episodes
[@lakatos1970; @meehl1990] has never been measured.

Formalising a theory also leaves untouched what @eronen2021 identify as reasons
why good psychological theories are hard to develop: the lack of robust
phenomena, the doubtful validity of constructs and the difficulty of finding
causal relations. The studies below do not address these. They address whether
the package's own outputs mean what its documentation says they mean. In
Messick's terms, Study 1 bears on the generalizability aspect of validity, here
across encoders, Study 2 on the external aspect and Study 3 on the
consequential aspect.

## The encoding pilot {#sec-pilot}

```{r}
#| label: inputs-pilot
# Encoding pilot: agent encoders of one model family each encoded the same
# verbal theories from summaries of about 600 words, analysed at commit
# f72ce4c. The values below are copied from the pilot's analysis tables; the
# table and column are named beside each.
pilot <- list(
  # tables/units_agreement.csv, row 'all': statements segmented from the
  # sources, statements made into the same kind of element by every encoder,
  # and Fleiss' kappa on the element type (fleiss_fine) and on whether the
  # statement carries a machine-readable claim (fleiss_claim)
  units = 73, units_same_element = 41,
  kappa_element = 0.643, kappa_claim = 0.559,
  # same table, rows per theory, fleiss_fine
  kappa_element_by_theory = c(0.671, 0.588, 0.658),
  # same table, codes_enc-1 to codes_enc-3, summed over encoders: P proposition,
  # PRc prediction with a claim, PRn prediction without one, PH phenomenon,
  # A assumption, B boundary condition, EV evidence, ALT rival, FF only in a
  # definition, mechanism or functional form
  codes = c(A = 27, ALT = 3, B = 24, EV = 3, FF = 12, P = 53, PH = 13,
            PRc = 50, PRn = 34),
  # tables/checklist_by_encoder.csv, aggregate (rows theories, columns encoders)
  scores = matrix(c(55.4, 60.9, 60.9,
                    57.2, 58.1, 56.3,
                    58.5, 60.2, 60.7), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("bilingual-rhm", "collaborative-cognitive-load",
                                    "health-habit"),
                                  c("enc-1", "enc-2", "enc-3"))),
  # tables/implications_agreement.csv, J_literal_basis for the pairs of files
  impl_jaccard = matrix(c(0.207, 0.077, 0.233,
                          0.659, 0.396, 0.396,
                          0.145, 0.052, 0.200), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  # tables/edge_agreement.csv, level 'directed', scope 'all', pairwise J
  edge_jaccard = matrix(c(0.556, 0.400, 0.714,
                          0.923, 0.586, 0.643,
                          0.471, 0.471, 0.857), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  # tables/structure.csv: constructs and propositions per file, and the
  # relation types of all propositions
  constructs = c(8, 7, 8, 19, 19, 17, 11, 11, 10),
  propositions = c(8, 6, 6, 26, 25, 21, 12, 13, 13),
  relation_types = c(increases = 64, decreases = 49, causes = 3, moderates = 14),
  # tables/checklist_item_spread.csv: item-by-theory cells with the same
  # status in every file
  item_cells_same = 34, item_cells = 36
)
n_pilot_enc <- ncol(pilot$scores)
n_pilot_th <- nrow(pilot$scores)
stopifnot(sum(pilot$codes) == n_pilot_enc * pilot$units,
          sum(pilot$relation_types) == sum(pilot$propositions),
          length(pilot$constructs) == length(pilot$scores))

# One-way analysis of variance of the scores, theories as groups.
oneway <- function(m) {
  k <- ncol(m); n <- nrow(m); gm <- mean(m)
  msb <- k * sum((rowMeans(m) - gm)^2) / (n - 1)
  msw <- sum((m - rowMeans(m))^2) / (n * (k - 1))
  list(icc1 = (msb - msw) / (msb + (k - 1) * msw), msb = msb, msw = msw)
}
pil <- oneway(pilot$scores)
```

The pilot asked `r nw(n_pilot_enc)` encoders to encode `r nw(n_pilot_th)` verbal
theories, the Revised Hierarchical Model of bilingual memory [@kroll2010],
collaborative cognitive load theory [@kirschner2018] and habit in health
behaviour [@gardner2015], from summaries of each source. Of the `r pilot$units`
statements segmented from the summaries, `r pilot$units_same_element` became the
same kind of element in all `r nw(n_pilot_enc)` files, with a Fleiss' kappa
[@fleiss1971] of `r f(pilot$kappa_element)`, and agreement on whether a
statement carried a machine-readable claim was lower (kappa
`r f(pilot$kappa_claim)`). Literal agreement on the implied conditional
independencies, after matching constructs, ranged from a Jaccard index of
`r f(min(pilot$impl_jaccard))` to `r f(max(pilot$impl_jaccard))` between pairs
of files. The checklist scores of the `r nw(length(pilot$scores))` files ranged
from `r f(min(pilot$scores), 1)` to `r f(max(pilot$scores), 1)`, and only
`r pct(pil$icc1)` of their variance lay between theories (ICC(1) =
`r f(pil$icc1, 3)`). The files had the same status on `r pilot$item_cells_same`
of `r pilot$item_cells` item-by-theory cells, mostly because the texts lacked
what several items ask for.

These values describe agents of one model family that read the same
documentation, working from summaries written by one author, with statements
segmented and constructs matched by one analyst. They say nothing about how
human researchers encode theories, and they offer no standard against which to
judge whether any encoding is faithful. They are used below as one input among
stated alternatives, never as the only basis of a sample size.

## Registration and structure

Each study is described under the headings that a preregistration needs: aims
and hypotheses, design, materials, participants and recruitment, procedure,
measures, analysis plan, sample size, inference criteria and limitations. The
plan of each study will be entered into the PRP-QUANT template of the Joint
Psychological Societies Preregistration Task Force [@bosnjak2022] and
registered before its data collection begins. Studies 1 and 2 share their
sample of theories and their coders and will be registered together. Study 3
is independent of the others and can run first. The analysis scripts will be
registered with the plans, and any deviation will be reported with its reason.

The author of this protocol maintains theoryforge and has an interest in
favourable results. To limit the consequences, the classification of known
groups, the expert ratings and the reader responses are collected by people who
do not see the package's outputs, the confirmatory analyses are run by an
analyst who does not maintain the package, from the registered scripts, on data
whose group labels and conditions are masked until the scripts have been run on
them, and every result is reported whatever its direction.

# Shared materials and methods {#sec-shared}

## Design constants

The constants below fix the design. They are choices, and the sample-size
sections show what follows from them.

```{r}
#| label: inputs-design
design <- list(
  coder_pool = 9,               # trained human coders
  coders_per_theory = 3,        # independent human encodings of each theory
  agent_runs = 3,               # independent agent encodings of each theory
  max_words = 3000,             # longest source passage, figures included
  unitise_check = 0.25,         # share of passages segmented twice
  classifiers = 3,              # panel that assigns the known groups
  hours_per_file = c(low = 4, mid = 6, high = 9),   # coder hours per file
  boot_reps = 2000,             # bootstrap resamples in the analyses
  experts_per_theory = 3,
  expert_pool = 15,
  experts_per_episode = 4,
  rating_scale = c(0, 10),      # expert ratings of each theory
  confidence_scale = c(1, 5),   # expert confidence in a verdict
  hours_per_rating = c(theory = 1, episode = 1.5),  # expert hours
  theories_per_reader = 2,      # Study 3 example theories per participant
  misread_items = 16,           # Study 3 statements that state a misreading
  correct_items = 8,            # Study 3 statements that state a correct reading
  output_types = 4,             # score, gate, dossier, appraisal
  attention_items = 2,
  alpha = 0.05,                 # two-sided; one-sided tests use alpha / 2
  power = 0.80,
  halfwidth = 0.10,             # target half-width of agreement coefficients
  rel_halfwidth = 0.25,         # target half-width of the SEM, relative to it
  icc_threshold = 0.50,         # theories account for half the score variance
  agree_level = 0.80,           # agreement at which a file may stand for the theory
  rho_null = 0.30,              # correlation the score must exceed (H2.1)
  rho_true = c(0.5, 0.7),       # true correlations considered for H2.1
  expert_icc_alt = 0.6,         # expert ICC above the reviewer value
  expert_kappa_design = 0.4,    # expert-expert kappa of the design scenario
  expert_kappa_high = 0.6,
  truth_tolerance = 0.20,       # tolerated rate of reading the score as truth
  ni_margin_or = 0.80,          # non-inferiority margin for correct readings
  sd_theory_logit = c(0.5, 1),  # Study 1: theory differences in coding accuracy
  sd_coder_logit = 0.3,         # Study 1: coder differences in coding accuracy
  coder_share = 0.25,           # share of encoding variance due to coders
  sd_expert_logit = 0.3,        # Study 2: expert differences in accuracy
  verdict_share = c(progressive = 1, neutral = 1, degenerating = 1) / 3,
  p0_low = 0.25,                # Study 3: lower baseline misreading probability
  or_design = 0.67,             # Study 3: design effect of the 0.8.0 wording
  or_large = 0.5,               # Study 3: larger alternative effect
  sd_reader = 1.0,              # Study 3: participant SD, logit scale
  sd_item = 0.8,                # Study 3: statement SD, logit scale
  sd_item_slope = 0.3,          # Study 3: SD of the wording effect over statements
  editor_share = 0.25,          # Study 3: share of editors sought
  reps_alpha = 500, reps_score = 200, reps_episode = 1000, reps_reader = 150,
  n_grid = c(24, 36, 48, 60, 72),      # theories, multiples of the 12 blocks
  ng_grid = 4:100,                     # theories per known group
  ep_grid = c(20, 30, 40, 60, 80),     # amendment episodes
  arm_grid = seq(50, 400, by = 25)     # readers per arm
)
known_groups <- c("corroborated", "refuted", "pseudoscientific")
ci_lab <- paste(100 * (1 - design$alpha), "per cent")
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - design$alpha / 2)
```

## Software versions

```{r}
#| label: inputs-repository
# Read from the repository at render time.
checklist <- yaml::read_yaml("../schema/rigor_checklist.yaml")
item_ids <- vapply(checklist$items, function(i) i$id, "")
blockers <- item_ids[vapply(checklist$items,
                            function(i) identical(i$severity_if_fail, "blocker"),
                            logical(1))]
pkg_version <- unname(read.dcf("../r/theoryforge/DESCRIPTION",
                               fields = "Version")[1, 1])
suppressMessages(pkgload::load_all("../r/theoryforge", quiet = TRUE))
example_files <- sort(list.files("../apps/examples", pattern = "[.]theory[.]yaml$",
                                 full.names = TRUE))
example_scores <- vapply(example_files,
                         function(p) tf_check(tf_read(p))$aggregate_score,
                         numeric(1))
names(example_scores) <- sub("[.]theory[.]yaml$", "", basename(example_files))
```

All encodings are run through one frozen release of the package, version
`r pkg_version` when this document was rendered, identified in each
registration by its commit. The checklist in the repository at rendering was
version `r checklist$schema_version`, with `r length(item_ids)` items of which
`r nw(length(blockers))` (`r and_list(paste0("'", blockers, "'"))`) can block
the gate. Study 3 also uses the release tagged v0.7.0. Outputs are computed in
R and checked in Python, since the two packages are specified to give the same
results.

## Sample of theories {#sec-sample}

Studies 1 and 2 use one sample of published verbal theories in the behavioural
sciences, drawn from three sources.

The first source is the database of behaviour change theories of @hale2020,
which lists theories with their primary sources and gives an independent
representation of each as construct-relationship triples. Theories are drawn
from it at random. The second source is a set of journals that publish
theoretical articles in psychology, searched over a span of years fixed at
registration for articles that propose or revise a named verbal theory. Two
screeners judge eligibility independently, and a third resolves disagreements.
Eligible articles are drawn at random. The third source supplies the known
groups (@sec-known-groups).

A theory is eligible when all of the following hold.

- A primary source by the theory's proponents states it in prose, with at least
  two constructs and at least one stated relation between them.
- The statement can be confined to a passage of at most
  `r f(design$max_words, 0)` words, including its figures and tables, on whose
  boundaries two screeners agree (a third resolves disagreements).
- The source is in English and can be given to every coder and expert.
- The theory has not been stated as a set of equations or as a computational
  model, since the question concerns verbal theories.
- The theory is not one of the pilot theories or the package's shipped
  examples, which serve for training.
- No member of the study team, coder or expert assigned to it is an author of
  the source.

## Known groups {#sec-known-groups}

Groups of `r and_list(known_groups)` theories are added to the sample, with
equal numbers in each (the number is set in @sec-s2-size).

- Corroborated: theories whose central risky prediction passed tests by groups
  independent of its proponents, documented in a systematic review, a
  multi-laboratory study or a registered replication published before sampling,
  with no unresolved failure of that prediction in tests of comparable quality.
- Refuted: theories whose central prediction failed in a high-powered
  registered or multi-laboratory test or in a systematic review, and which later
  reviews describe as refuted or as abandoned in its original form.
- Pseudoscientific: doctrines presented by their proponents as scientific
  explanations of behaviour, which a scientific body's statement or a
  peer-reviewed review describes as lacking scientific support, and whose
  proponents have met reported failures by changing the doctrine without
  stating new tests or by rejecting the tests. A written statement by the
  proponents of a length comparable with the other sources must exist.

Candidates for each group are listed from structured searches of review
literature, with search strings fixed at registration. A panel of
`r nw(design$classifiers)` methodologists, who are neither coders nor Study 2
experts, assigns each candidate to a group or to none by the criteria above,
independently and before any candidate is encoded. A candidate enters a group
only when a majority of the panel assigns it there, and the panel's agreement
is reported. The classification rests on the empirical and historical record of
each theory and is made without reference to how completely its source
specifies it, so that the groups are not defined by the quantity they are used
to validate.

## Source passages and statements

For each theory, two screeners fix the passage of the primary source that
states it. A trained unitiser segments the passage into statements, each
stating one construct, relation, condition, prediction or assumption. A second
unitiser independently segments a random `r pct(design$unitise_check)` of the
passages, and the agreement between the two segmentations is reported. The
coders then work from the segmented passages, so that disagreement about where
a statement begins does not enter the agreement on what it became.

## Written encoding protocol and coder training {#sec-encoding-protocol}

Before Study 1 begins, the encoding protocol will be written down and frozen.
It states conventions for the choices that produced most disagreement in the
pilot:

- when a stated relation also becomes a prediction;
- how an interaction is encoded, since encoding it as `moderates` leaves the
  moderated relation unsigned;
- how a feedback loop is encoded;
- that a mechanism field is filled only when the text gives a reason;
- that no bound, measure or rival is written that the text does not state.

For each statement, the coder records which
element or elements of the file it became, using the pilot's categories
(proposition, prediction with or without a machine-readable claim, phenomenon,
assumption, boundary condition, evidence, rival, wording only) and a further
category for a statement left out.

Coders train on the pilot theories. They receive feedback on the format of
their files and on the use of the protocol, and none on content, since feedback
on content would teach them the trainers' readings and raise their agreement
above what independent users of the protocol would reach. A coder is admitted
after completing the training files with full validation passing. The
reliability estimated in Study 1 therefore applies to researchers trained with
a written protocol, which is more than most users of the package receive.

## Construct matching

Comparing two files requires deciding which construct in one corresponds to
which construct in the other. Two adjudicators, who are not coders, match the
constructs of the files of each theory independently, without knowing which
coder produced which file. Their agreement is reported, disagreements are
resolved by discussion, and every analysis that depends on matching is repeated
with each adjudicator's own matching.

## Agent encoders {#sec-agents}

Each theory is also encoded `r nw(design$agent_runs)` times by an agent: a
language model given the source passage, the written encoding protocol and the
package's documentation, with the package available to validate its files. Each
run starts in a fresh session and sees no human encoding and no other run. The
model's identifier and version, the date and the full instructions are fixed at
registration and archived. The pilot's encoders were agents of one model
family, which may share readings that independent humans would not, so
agreement among agent runs is reported separately and is not treated as
exchangeable with agreement among humans.

## Inputs for the sample-size calculations {#sec-inputs}

The sample sizes below are justified by the precision they give and, for the
hypotheses that are tested, by their power [@lakens2022]. Where no closed form
fits the design, the operating characteristics are estimated by simulation with
fixed seeds, and Monte Carlo standard errors are reported [@morris2019]. The
pilot inputs are in @sec-pilot and the external ones in @sec-background. Two
further inputs come from analyses of the shipped example files.

```{r}
#| label: inputs-encoding
encoding_sd <- list(
  # Standard deviation of the checklist score over combinations of encoding
  # choices that leave one theory's statements unchanged, for the shipped
  # panic-network v1 and modality-switching files: with content-preserving
  # choices only, and with all choices, including one that deletes
  # construct-level boundary conditions.
  content = c(panic_v1 = 3.32, modality = 3.36),
  all = c(panic_v1 = 4.81, modality = 5.49)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: inputs-derived
sd_theory <- c(
  pilot = sqrt(max(0, (pil$msb - pil$msw) / n_pilot_enc)),
  examples = sd(example_scores),
  pooled = sd(c(rowMeans(pilot$scores), example_scores)))
sem_in <- c(pilot = sqrt(pil$msw),
            content = mean(encoding_sd$content),
            all = mean(encoding_sd$all))
sdd <- function(sem) z_crit * sqrt(2) * sem
sb <- function(icc, k) k * icc / (1 + (k - 1) * icc)
icc_mid <- sd_theory[["examples"]]^2 /
  (sd_theory[["examples"]]^2 + sem_in[["content"]]^2)
units_per_theory <- round(pilot$units / n_pilot_th)
code_share <- pilot$codes / sum(pilot$codes)
pairs_total <- sum(choose(pilot$constructs, 2))
edge_joined <- sum(pilot$propositions) / pairs_total
edge_share <- c(none = 1 - edge_joined,
                rep(edge_joined * pilot$relation_types /
                      sum(pilot$relation_types) / 2, each = 2))
edge_units <- round(pairs_total / length(pilot$constructs))
impl_sd <- sd(rowMeans(pilot$impl_jaccard))
edge_sd <- sd(rowMeans(pilot$edge_jaccard))
p_hoekstra <- external$false_endorsed / external$false_items
```

Three inputs need comment. First, the spread of checklist scores between
theories. The pilot's analysis of variance gives a between-theory standard
deviation of `r f(sd_theory[["pilot"]])` points. The
`r nw(length(example_scores))` example theories shipped with the apps, each a
published theory encoded by one person, have scores from
`r f(min(example_scores), 1)` to `r f(max(example_scores), 1)` with a standard
deviation of `r f(sd_theory[["examples"]])` points, which includes that
person's encoding noise. Pooling the pilot theories' means with the examples
gives `r f(sd_theory[["pooled"]])` points, which mixes encoders as well as
theories and is used as the widest plausible spread. Second, the encoding
noise. The pilot's within-theory standard deviation is
`r f(sem_in[["pilot"]])` points. Over combinations of content-preserving
encoding choices for two shipped theories it is `r f(sem_in[["content"]])`
points on average, and `r f(sem_in[["all"]])` when a choice that deletes
construct-level boundary conditions is included. The middle values,
`r f(sd_theory[["examples"]])` and `r f(sem_in[["content"]])`, define the
design scenario, under which theories would account for `r pct(icc_mid)` of the
variance of a single encoding's score. Third, the human baselines.
@bornmann2010 found a mean reliability of `r f(external$reviewer_icc)` on the
intraclass correlation scale and a mean Cohen's kappa of
`r f(external$reviewer_kappa)` between journal reviewers judging the same
manuscript. These values concern recommendations on manuscripts, not encodings
of theories, and serve as a floor: an encoding procedure whose agreement did
not exceed them would be no more reproducible than unstructured expert
judgement of scientific documents.

## Coder assignment {#sec-assignment}

```{r}
#| label: coder-design
# Steiner triple system on 9 coders: 12 blocks of 3, every pair of coders
# together in exactly one block. Theories are assigned to blocks at random.
sts9 <- rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(4, 5, 6), c(7, 8, 9), c(1, 4, 7), c(2, 5, 8),
              c(3, 6, 9), c(1, 5, 9), c(2, 6, 7), c(3, 4, 8), c(1, 6, 8),
              c(2, 4, 9), c(3, 5, 7))
# Balanced incomplete block design on 6 coders: 10 blocks of 3, every pair
# together in exactly two blocks (used only for comparison).
bibd6 <- rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(1, 2, 4), c(1, 3, 5), c(1, 4, 6), c(1, 5, 6),
               c(2, 3, 6), c(2, 4, 5), c(2, 5, 6), c(3, 4, 5), c(3, 4, 6))
pair_lambda <- function(b) {
  unique(as.vector(table(apply(b, 1, function(r)
    combn(sort(r), 2, paste, collapse = "-")))))
}
stopifnot(max(sts9) == design$coder_pool,
          ncol(sts9) == design$coders_per_theory,
          length(pair_lambda(sts9)) == 1, length(pair_lambda(bibd6)) == 1,
          length(unique(as.vector(table(sts9)))) == 1,
          all(design$n_grid %% nrow(sts9) == 0))
```

Each theory is encoded independently by `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` of
`r nw(design$coder_pool)` coders. The assignment follows a Steiner triple
system: the `r nrow(sts9)` triples of coders are used equally often, so that
every coder encodes the same number of theories and every pair of coders shares
the same number of theories (`r nw(pair_lambda(sts9))` in each cycle of
`r nrow(sts9)` theories). Coders are thus crossed with theories in an
incomplete design, for which @tenhove2024 give guidance on choosing and
estimating intraclass correlations. A pool of `r nw(design$coder_pool)` rather
than `r nw(max(bibd6))` coders spreads the work and estimates stable
differences between coders from more coders, and @sec-s1-size shows how much
that changes the precision.

# Claims and hypotheses {#sec-claims}

@tbl-claims lists the claims that the studies examine and the result that would
count against each. They are claims that a reader of the documentation could
reasonably take the package to make, including some that version 0.8.0 no
longer makes in so many words, because the outputs invite them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-claims
#| tbl-cap: "Claims examined, the study that examines each and the result that would count against it."
claims <- data.frame(
  Claim = c(
    "C1. A file encodes the theory, so that what the package derives from it belongs to the theory and not to one encoder's choices.",
    "C2. Differences between the checklist scores of two theories reflect the theories rather than their encoders.",
    "C3. The checklist score and the item statuses track how completely and how testably experts judge a theory to be specified.",
    "C4. The labels progressive, degenerating and neutral correspond to what an expert applying Lakatos's terms would conclude about the same amendment.",
    "C5. In the 0.8.0 wording, readers do not take the score, the gate, the dossier or the appraisal for judgements of truth or quality."),
  Study = c("1", "1", "2", "2", "3"),
  `Counts against it` = c(
    paste0("Agreement among independent human coders on the elements or the signed edges whose ", ci_lab, " interval lies below ", f(design$agree_level), " (H1.1 and H1.2)."),
    paste0("A ", ci_lab, " interval for ICC(A,1), the share of score variance due to theories, that lies below ", f(design$icc_threshold), ", or a smallest detectable difference larger than the differences users are told to read (H1.3)."),
    paste0("A correlation with expert ratings of completeness whose ", ci_lab, " interval lies below ", f(design$rho_null), ", or pseudoscientific theories that score no lower than corroborated and refuted ones (H2.1 and H2.2)."),
    "Agreement of the package's verdicts with experts that is reliably lower than the agreement of experts with each other (H2.3).",
    paste0("An odds ratio of misreading, 0.8.0 against 0.7.0 wording, whose ", ci_lab, " interval lies wholly above the design effect of ", f(design$or_design), ", or a rate of reading the score as truth whose lower limit exceeds ", pct(design$truth_tolerance), " (H3.1 and H3.2).")),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(claims)
```

# Study 1: encoding reliability {#sec-study1}

## Aims and hypotheses

Study 1 estimates how far independent human coders who follow the written
protocol produce the same file from the same verbal theory, at each level at
which the package reads the file: the elements each statement becomes, the
signed edges of the causal graph, the predictions with machine-readable claims,
the derived implications and claim verdicts, the checklist item statuses and
the checklist score. It compares this agreement with the reviewer baseline,
with the agreement of Study 2's experts on the same theories and with agent
encoders. The study is reported following the GRRAS guidelines
[@kottner2011].

The primary hypotheses are:

- H1.1: agreement among human coders on the element each statement becomes,
  measured by Krippendorff's alpha, exceeds the reviewer kappa of
  `r f(external$reviewer_kappa)`.
- H1.2: agreement among human coders on the status of each pair of shared
  constructs in the causal graph (no edge, or an edge with its direction and
  sign) exceeds the reviewer kappa.
- H1.3: the share of the variance of the checklist score due to theories,
  ICC(A,1) in the notation of @mcgraw1996, exceeds the reviewer reliability of
  `r f(external$reviewer_icc)`.

The hypotheses state a floor. The claims of @tbl-claims need more, and the
inference criteria (@sec-s1-inference) state what each result would mean for
them. Claim C1 is supported only if agreement on elements and edges reaches
`r f(design$agree_level)`, the level at which we take a file to stand for the
theory, and is contradicted if the upper `r ci_lab` limit lies below that
level. Claim C2 is supported only if the lower limit of ICC(A,1) exceeds
`r f(design$icc_threshold)`, so that theories account for more than half of
the variance of a single encoding's score, and is contradicted if the upper
limit lies below it. These levels are our conventions, stated in advance, and
other readers may set them elsewhere. At an alpha of `r f(design$agree_level)`
on the element types, with the pilot's distribution of types, about
`r pct((1 - design$agree_level) * (1 - sum(code_share^2)))` of pairs of codings
of a statement would disagree.

## Design

Study 1 is a reliability study in which `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)`
human coders and `r nw(design$agent_runs)` agent runs encode each theory of the
shared sample independently, with coders crossed with theories in the incomplete
design of @sec-assignment. There is no manipulation.

## Materials

The materials are the segmented source passages of the sample of theories
(@sec-sample and @sec-known-groups), the written encoding protocol, the
package's documentation at the frozen release and a spreadsheet in which coders
record, for each statement, the element or elements it became.

## Participants and recruitment

Coders are doctoral students, postdoctoral researchers or research assistants
with training in a behavioural science and in research methods, recruited by
advertisement in the University of Oxford and in partner institutions. They are
paid for their time at the University's rate for research assistance. People
who have contributed to theoryforge, or who have used it before, are not
eligible. The agent encoders are described in @sec-agents.

## Procedure

After training (@sec-encoding-protocol), each coder receives the passages
assigned to them in a random order. A coder works alone, may consult the
package's documentation and the written protocol and may run the package to
validate the file, and may not consult other coders or any other encoding of
the theory. For each passage the coder writes a theory file, records the
element each statement became, records the time spent and, for each element,
how confident they are that the text supports it. A file is submitted once full
validation passes or once the coder has recorded why it does not. Questions
about the protocol go to a coordinator, who answers them in writing to all
coders at once, and the questions and answers are archived.

## Measures {#sec-s1-measures}

All outputs are computed with the frozen release from each submitted file.

- Element type. For each statement, the category of the element it became
  (@sec-encoding-protocol). Agreement is measured by Krippendorff's alpha for
  nominal data [@hayes2007] over statements, and by Fleiss' kappa for
  comparison with the pilot.
- Signed edges. For each unordered pair of constructs that the coders of a
  theory share after matching, its status: no edge, an edge in either direction
  with sign increases, decreases or unsigned causes, or a moderation. Agreement
  is measured by alpha over pairs, and by the mean pairwise Jaccard index of the
  sets of signed edges.
- Predictions with claims. The set of claims (cause, effect, kind and sign)
  stated by each file, compared by the mean pairwise Jaccard index.
- Derived implications. The basis set of implied conditional independencies,
  compared literally by the Jaccard index after matching constructs, and the
  independence model over the constructs that all coders of a theory share,
  compared by alpha over triples (independent or not, given each conditioning
  set), as in the pilot.
- Claim verdicts. For each claim stated in at least two files of a theory, the
  verdict of `entailments()` (entailed, contradicted, left open or not
  evaluated), compared by alpha with missing values for files that do not state
  the claim.
- Checklist item statuses. For each item, the status in each file (pass, warn,
  fail or not applicable), compared by alpha and by Gwet's AC1, which behaves
  better than kappa when one status is far more common than the others
  [@gwet2008; @feinstein1990].
- Checklist score. The score of each file, analysed as a continuous measure.
- Secondary measures: the agreement of the two unitisers, the time per file,
  the share of files that pass full validation, the coders' confidence and, for
  the theories drawn from @hale2020, the agreement of each file's
  construct-relationship pairs with that study's representation.

## Analysis plan {#sec-s1-analysis}

Agreement coefficients are computed over all theories, with statements, pairs
or triples as units and coders as raters. Krippendorff's alpha accommodates
any number of coders and missing values [@hayes2007]. Because units are nested
in theories and coders are crossed with theories, intervals come from a
bootstrap that resamples theories and coders independently, the pigeonhole
bootstrap of @owen2007, with `r f(design$boot_reps, 0)` resamples. Jaccard
indices are averaged over coder pairs within a theory and then over theories,
with intervals from the same bootstrap.

The checklist score is analysed with a linear mixed model with crossed random
intercepts for theories and coders, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood
with lme4 [@bates2015]:

$$y_{ij} = \mu + t_i + c_j + e_{ij}, \quad t_i \sim N(0, \sigma_t^2), \quad
c_j \sim N(0, \sigma_c^2), \quad e_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2).$$

Coders are treated as random, as @tenhove2024 recommend for interrater
reliability. From the variance components the analysis reports three
quantities.

- ICC(A,1) $= \sigma_t^2 / (\sigma_t^2 + \sigma_c^2 + \sigma_e^2)$, the
  agreement form in the terms of @shrout1979 and @mcgraw1996, which fits
  because readers compare the scores of theories encoded by different people.
- The standard error of measurement of a single encoding,
  SEM $= \sqrt{\sigma_c^2 + \sigma_e^2}$.
- The smallest detectable difference between two theories encoded by different
  coders, SDD $= z\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{SEM}$ with $z$ = `r f(z_crit)`.
 Intervals
come from a parametric bootstrap of the fitted model with
`r f(design$boot_reps, 0)` replicates, and from the pigeonhole bootstrap as a
check. The model is refitted with fixed effects for the known groups and the
sampling source, so that the ICC is also reported within groups.

Human-human agreement is compared with the reviewer baseline as H1.1 to H1.3
state. It is compared with the agreement of Study 2's experts on the same
theories by the difference between the ICC of the score across coders and the
ICC of the experts' completeness ratings across experts, and between the alpha
of each item status across coders and the alpha of the experts' judgements of
the corresponding item, with intervals from a bootstrap that resamples
theories, coders and experts. Agent encodings are compared with human ones by
the difference between agent-human and human-human agreement on each measure,
and agent-agent agreement is reported separately.

A coder who leaves is replaced, and their unfinished theories are reassigned so
that each theory keeps `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` human encodings. The
mixed model and alpha both use all available encodings and assume that
encodings are missing at random given the theory and the coder. A file that
never passes full validation is analysed as submitted, and the share of such
files is reported. A statement left without a category is coded as left out.

## Sample size {#sec-s1-size}

The number of theories is set by the precision of the agreement coefficients
and of the SEM. Agreement on element types and on edges is simulated by a model
in which each coder reproduces a statement's true category with a probability
that varies between theories and between coders on the logit scale (standard
deviations `r and_list(f(design$sd_theory_logit, 1))` for theories and
`r f(design$sd_coder_logit, 1)` for coders) and otherwise picks a category at
random from the observed distribution. The intercept is calibrated so that the
population value of alpha equals each target: the pilot's kappa on element
types (`r f(pilot$kappa_element)`), its lower kappa on claims
(`r f(pilot$kappa_claim)`) and the level claim C1 needs
(`r f(design$agree_level)`). Element types follow the pilot's distribution with
`r units_per_theory` statements per theory. Edges follow the pilot's
structure: of the `r f(pairs_total, 0)` pairs of constructs in the pilot files,
`r pct(edge_joined)` were joined by a proposition, and each theory contributes
`r edge_units` pairs.

```{r}
#| label: functions-agreement
# Gauss-Hermite nodes and weights for a standard normal (Golub-Welsch).
gh_nodes <- function(n = 40) {
  i <- seq_len(n - 1)
  J <- matrix(0, n, n)
  J[cbind(i, i + 1)] <- sqrt(i)
  J[cbind(i + 1, i)] <- sqrt(i)
  e <- eigen(J, symmetric = TRUE)
  list(x = e$values, w = e$vectors[1, ]^2)
}
GH <- gh_nodes()
# With accuracy q and errors drawn from the category distribution, two coders
# agree beyond chance by q * q', so the population alpha is E[q q'] for two
# coders of the same theory.
pop_alpha <- function(eta, sd_t, sd_c) {
  inner <- vapply(GH$x * sd_t,
                  function(b) sum(GH$w * plogis(eta + b + GH$x * sd_c)), 0)
  sum(GH$w * inner^2)
}
calibrate_eta <- function(target, sd_t, sd_c) {
  uniroot(function(e) pop_alpha(e, sd_t, sd_c) - target, c(-8, 12))$root
}
# Krippendorff's alpha, nominal, every unit coded by every column.
alpha_nominal <- function(codes) {
  m <- ncol(codes)
  agree <- 0
  for (a in 1:(m - 1)) for (b in (a + 1):m) {
    agree <- agree + sum(codes[, a] == codes[, b])
  }
  d_obs <- 1 - 2 * agree / (nrow(codes) * m * (m - 1))
  nc <- tabulate(codes, nbins = max(codes))
  n <- sum(nc)
  d_exp <- 1 - sum(nc * (nc - 1)) / (n * (n - 1))
  1 - d_obs / d_exp
}
sim_alpha <- function(n_t, units, share, target, sd_t, sd_c, blocks, reps) {
  eta <- calibrate_eta(target, sd_t, sd_c)
  ncat <- length(share); K <- max(blocks); m <- ncol(blocks)
  assign <- blocks[rep_len(seq_len(nrow(blocks)), n_t), , drop = FALSE]
  theory <- rep(seq_len(n_t), each = units)
  est <- replicate(reps, {
    b <- rnorm(n_t, 0, sd_t)
    d <- rnorm(K, 0, sd_c)
    truth <- sample.int(ncat, n_t * units, TRUE, share)
    codes <- vapply(seq_len(m), function(k) {
      q <- plogis(eta + b[theory] + d[assign[theory, k]])
      ifelse(runif(length(q)) < q, truth,
             sample.int(ncat, length(q), TRUE, share))
    }, integer(n_t * units))
    alpha_nominal(codes)
  })
  c(mean = mean(est), sd = sd(est))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-agreement
set.seed(20261125)
# Sampling noise of one theory's coefficient in the pilot's setting: one
# theory, its statements, three encoders with equal accuracy.
pilot_noise <- sim_alpha(1, units_per_theory, code_share, pilot$kappa_element,
                         0, 0, matrix(seq_len(n_pilot_enc), nrow = 1),
                         design$reps_alpha)[["sd"]]
grid_a <- expand.grid(n = design$n_grid,
                      target = c(pilot$kappa_claim, pilot$kappa_element,
                                 design$agree_level),
                      sd_t = design$sd_theory_logit,
                      kind = c("element", "edge"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res_a <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_a)), function(i) {
  g <- grid_a[i, ]
  if (g$kind == "element") {
    sim_alpha(g$n, units_per_theory, code_share, g$target, g$sd_t,
              design$sd_coder_logit, sts9, design$reps_alpha)
  } else {
    sim_alpha(g$n, edge_units, edge_share, g$target, g$sd_t,
              design$sd_coder_logit, sts9, design$reps_alpha)
  }
}, numeric(2)))
grid_a$mean <- res_a[, "mean"]
grid_a$sd <- res_a[, "sd"]
grid_a$halfwidth <- z_crit * grid_a$sd
# Monte Carlo standard error of a standard deviation estimated from R replicates.
grid_a$mcse_hw <- z_crit * grid_a$sd / sqrt(2 * (design$reps_alpha - 1))
ok_a <- with(grid_a, aggregate(halfwidth <= design$halfwidth,
                               list(n = n, kind = kind, sd_t = sd_t), all))
first_ok <- function(kind) {
  n_ok <- ok_a$n[ok_a$kind == kind & ok_a$sd_t == min(design$sd_theory_logit) &
                   ok_a$x]
  if (length(n_ok)) min(n_ok) else max(design$n_grid)
}
n_alpha <- first_ok("element")
n_alpha_edge <- first_ok("edge")
```

The pilot's per-theory kappas had a standard deviation of
`r f(sd(pilot$kappa_element_by_theory), 3)`. Sampling alone would give about
`r f(pilot_noise, 3)` for one theory of `r units_per_theory` statements coded
by `r nw(n_pilot_enc)` equally accurate encoders, so the pilot shows
`r if (sd(pilot$kappa_element_by_theory) <= pilot_noise) "no" else "some"`
difference between theories beyond noise, and the theory standard deviations
assumed here allow for more than the pilot shows, as a more varied sample would
need.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-alpha
#| tbl-cap: "Expected half-width of the interval for alpha, the critical value times the standard deviation of the estimates over replicates, by number of theories, target alpha and theory standard deviation on the logit scale."
tab_a <- reshape(grid_a[, c("kind", "sd_t", "target", "n", "halfwidth")],
                 idvar = c("kind", "sd_t", "target"), timevar = "n",
                 direction = "wide")
names(tab_a) <- c("Units", "Theory SD", "Target alpha",
                  paste(design$n_grid, "theories"))
tab_a[, -(1:3)] <- lapply(tab_a[, -(1:3)], f, d = 3)
tab_a$`Target alpha` <- f(tab_a$`Target alpha`)
knitr::kable(tab_a, row.names = FALSE)
```

With `r nw(design$coder_pool)` coders, the coder effects do not average out as
theories are added, so the half-width falls more slowly than the inverse square
root of the number of theories. Under the smaller theory standard deviation,
the half-width of alpha on element types is at most `r f(design$halfwidth)` at
every target with `r n_alpha` theories, and the half-width on edges with
`r n_alpha_edge` theories. The Monte Carlo standard errors of the half-widths
are at most `r f(max(grid_a$mcse_hw), 4)`.

The Jaccard indices have no chance correction and are summarised by their mean
over theories, whose standard error is dominated by differences between
theories. Here a closed form fits: with a between-theory standard deviation
$s$, a half-width $h$ needs $n = (z\,s/h)^2$ theories. The pilot gives
$s$ = `r f(impl_sd, 3)` for the implied independencies and `r f(edge_sd, 3)`
for the signed edges. Half and one and a half times the implications value are
used as alternatives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-jaccard
#| tbl-cap: "Theories needed for a given half-width h of the mean Jaccard index, by between-theory standard deviation."
n_jacc <- function(s, h) ceiling((z_crit * s / h)^2)
s_alt <- c(`pilot, signed edges` = edge_sd, `pilot, implications` = impl_sd,
           `half the implications value` = impl_sd / 2,
           `one and a half times it` = 1.5 * impl_sd)
h_alt <- c(design$halfwidth / 2, design$halfwidth)
tab_j <- data.frame(names(s_alt), f(s_alt, 3),
                    vapply(h_alt, function(h) n_jacc(s_alt, h),
                           numeric(length(s_alt))))
names(tab_j) <- c("Standard deviation", "s", paste("h =", f(h_alt)))
knitr::kable(tab_j, row.names = FALSE)
n_impl <- n_jacc(impl_sd, design$halfwidth)
```

The checklist score is simulated from the mixed model of @sec-s1-analysis in
the incomplete design, for every combination of the three between-theory
standard deviations and the three encoding standard deviations of
@sec-inputs, with `r pct(design$coder_share)` of the encoding variance due to
stable differences between coders. Each replicate is analysed as the real data
will be, by restricted maximum likelihood, and the distribution of the
estimates over `r design$reps_score` replicates gives the precision. Fits that
raise a warning are kept and counted.

```{r}
#| label: functions-score
ctrl <- lmerControl(check.conv.singular = .makeCC(action = "ignore", tol = 1e-4))
sim_score <- function(n_t, sd_t, sem, coder_share, blocks, reps) {
  K <- max(blocks)
  assign <- blocks[rep_len(seq_len(nrow(blocks)), n_t), , drop = FALSE]
  d <- data.frame(theory = factor(rep(seq_len(n_t), each = ncol(blocks))),
                  coder = factor(as.vector(t(assign)), levels = seq_len(K)))
  sd_c <- sqrt(coder_share) * sem
  sd_e <- sqrt(1 - coder_share) * sem
  gen <- function() {
    rnorm(n_t, 0, sd_t)[d$theory] + rnorm(K, 0, sd_c)[d$coder] +
      rnorm(nrow(d), 0, sd_e)
  }
  d$y <- gen()
  fit <- lmer(y ~ 1 + (1 | theory) + (1 | coder), data = d, REML = TRUE,
              control = ctrl)
  est <- t(replicate(reps, {
    warned <- FALSE
    f_r <- withCallingHandlers(refit(fit, gen()), warning = function(w) {
      warned <<- TRUE
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    })
    v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(f_r))
    v <- setNames(v$vcov, v$grp)
    c(icc = unname(v["theory"] / sum(v)),
      sem = unname(sqrt(v["coder"] + v["Residual"])), warned = warned)
  }))
  icc_sd <- sd(est[, "icc"])
  c(n = n_t, true_icc = sd_t^2 / (sd_t^2 + sem^2),
    icc_mean = mean(est[, "icc"]), icc_sd = icc_sd,
    icc_lo = unname(quantile(est[, "icc"], design$alpha / 2)),
    icc_hi = unname(quantile(est[, "icc"], 1 - design$alpha / 2)),
    sem_mean = mean(est[, "sem"]), sem_sd = sd(est[, "sem"]),
    sem_rel_hw = z_crit * sd(est[, "sem"]) / sem,
    p_floor = mean(est[, "icc"] - z_crit * icc_sd > external$reviewer_icc),
    p_half = mean(est[, "icc"] - z_crit * icc_sd > design$icc_threshold),
    warned = sum(est[, "warned"]))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-score
set.seed(20261126)
grid_s <- expand.grid(n = design$n_grid, sd_t = names(sd_theory),
                      sem = names(sem_in), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res_s <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_s)), function(i) {
  g <- grid_s[i, ]
  sim_score(g$n, sd_theory[[g$sd_t]], sem_in[[g$sem]], design$coder_share,
            sts9, design$reps_score)
}, numeric(12)))
grid_s <- cbind(grid_s, res_s[, -1])
mid <- grid_s$sd_t == "examples" & grid_s$sem == "content"
n_sem_ok <- grid_s$n[mid & grid_s$sem_rel_hw <= design$rel_halfwidth]
n_sem <- if (length(n_sem_ok)) min(n_sem_ok) else max(design$n_grid)
# The smaller coder pool, for comparison, at the largest number in the grid
# that both designs' block counts divide.
n_cmp <- max(design$n_grid[design$n_grid %% nrow(bibd6) == 0])
cmp <- rbind(
  nine = unlist(grid_s[mid & grid_s$n == n_cmp, c("icc_sd", "sem_rel_hw")]),
  six = sim_score(n_cmp, sd_theory[["examples"]], sem_in[["content"]],
                  design$coder_share, bibd6,
                  design$reps_score)[c("icc_sd", "sem_rel_hw")])
# Monte Carlo standard error of the difference between two such SDs.
cmp_mcse <- sqrt(sum(cmp[, "icc_sd"]^2 / (2 * (design$reps_score - 1))))
pool_sentence <- if (abs(cmp["nine", "icc_sd"] - cmp["six", "icc_sd"]) <
                     2 * cmp_mcse) {
  paste("The difference in the ICC is within twice its Monte Carlo standard",
        "error, so under this scenario the larger pool serves mainly to spread",
        "the work and to estimate coder differences from more coders, which",
        "would matter more if they were larger than assumed.")
} else {
  paste("The larger pool estimates coder differences from more coders, which",
        "narrows the interval.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-score
#| tbl-cap: "Simulated estimation of the checklist score's reliability. True ICC is the share of variance due to theories; the range column holds the central estimates at the interval's level; the SEM half-width is relative to the true SEM; the last two columns give the approximate probability that the lower interval limit exceeds the reviewer reliability and one half."
tab_s <- data.frame(
  `Theory SD` = paste0(grid_s$sd_t, " (", f(sd_theory[grid_s$sd_t]), ")"),
  `Encoding SD` = paste0(grid_s$sem, " (", f(sem_in[grid_s$sem]), ")"),
  Theories = grid_s$n, `True ICC` = f(grid_s$true_icc),
  `ICC SD` = f(grid_s$icc_sd, 3),
  `Range of estimates` = paste(f(grid_s$icc_lo), "to", f(grid_s$icc_hi)),
  `SEM half-width` = f(grid_s$sem_rel_hw),
  `P(> reviewer)` = f(grid_s$p_floor),
  `P(> one half)` = f(grid_s$p_half), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab_s, row.names = FALSE)
```

Three things follow from @tbl-score. First, the reliability of the score depends
mostly on how much the theories in the sample differ, which no sample size can
change. If published verbal theories differ as little as the pilot theories or
the app examples, the score's ICC will be low whatever the number of coders, and
the study will show that. Second, under the design scenario, the SEM is
estimated within `r pct(design$rel_halfwidth)` of its value with `r n_sem`
theories. Third, at `r n_cmp` theories under the design scenario, the standard
deviation of the ICC estimate is `r f(cmp["nine", "icc_sd"], 3)` with
`r nw(design$coder_pool)` coders and `r f(cmp["six", "icc_sd"], 3)` with
`r nw(max(bibd6))`, and the relative half-width of the SEM is
`r f(cmp["nine", "sem_rel_hw"])` against `r f(cmp["six", "sem_rel_hw"])`.
`r pool_sentence` The power columns treat the replication standard deviation as
a known standard error and are approximate. Of the
`r f(nrow(grid_s) * design$reps_score, 0)` simulated fits,
`r sum(grid_s$warned)` raised a warning.

```{r}
#| label: n-study1
round_up <- function(x, k) k * ceiling(x / k)
n_study1 <- round_up(max(n_alpha, n_sem, n_impl), nrow(sts9))
```

Study 1 needs the largest of the numbers of theories required for alpha on
element types (`r n_alpha`), for the SEM (`r n_sem`) and for the mean Jaccard
index of the implications (`r n_impl`), rounded up to a multiple of the
`r nrow(sts9)` blocks of the coder design, which is `r n_study1`. Study 2 may
need more, and the final number is set in @sec-final-n.

## Inference criteria {#sec-s1-inference}

H1.1 to H1.3 are tested one-sided at level `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)` with the
Holm procedure across the family: the $p$ values are ordered from the smallest,
the $k$-th smallest is compared with `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)` divided by
$m + 1 - k$, where $m$ is the number of hypotheses in the family, and testing
stops at the first that is not below its threshold. Whatever the tests show,
each coefficient is reported with its `r ci_lab` interval and read against the
levels of @tbl-claims. For alpha on elements and on edges, a lower limit at or
above `r f(design$agree_level)` supports claim C1, an upper limit below it
contradicts C1, and anything else leaves C1 open. For the score, a lower limit
of ICC(A,1) above `r f(design$icc_threshold)` supports claim C2, an upper limit
below it contradicts C2, and the SDD with its interval is reported as the
smallest difference between two theories' scores that the data allow a reader
to interpret. If C1 is contradicted, the documentation must present every
derived output as a property of one encoding, and if C2 is contradicted, it
must advise against comparing the scores of theories encoded by different
people.

## Limitations

The theories are a sample of verbal theories in the behavioural sciences, and
the estimates may not transfer to other fields or to theories stated formally.
The ICC is a property of the sample as well as of the procedure, so the SEM and
the SDD, which do not depend on how much the sampled theories differ, are the
more transferable results. Coders follow a written protocol and receive
training, so agreement among untrained users is likely to be lower. Matching
constructs and segmenting statements are judgements, and their own agreement
limits what the coefficients can show. Agreement is not accuracy: coders could
agree on a reading the theory's authors would reject, which only the
comparison with @hale2020 for a subset, and Study 2, address. Agent encoders
change quickly, so their results describe one model at one date.

# Study 2: criterion and known-groups validity {#sec-study2}

## Aims and hypotheses

Study 2 asks whether the checklist and the appraisal agree with experts who
judge the same theories and amendments without seeing the package's outputs.
Part A concerns theories: the checklist score, the item statuses and a revised
profile are compared with blind expert ratings of how completely and how
testably each theory is specified, and the scores of known groups are
compared. Part B concerns amendment episodes: the verdicts of
`appraise_amendment()` are compared with blind expert appraisals.

The primary hypotheses are:

- H2.1: the correlation between a theory's checklist score (the mean over its
  `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` encodings) and the experts' mean rating of
  how completely it is specified is positive. Claim C3 needs more than that.
  Even a correlation of `r f(design$rho_null)` would leave
  `r pct(1 - design$rho_null^2)` of the variance of the expert rating
  unexplained, so C3 is supported only if the lower `r ci_lab` limit exceeds
  `r f(design$rho_null)`, and it is contradicted if the upper limit lies below
  that value.
- H2.2: pseudoscientific theories have lower checklist scores than corroborated
  and refuted theories taken together. A refuted theory was testable enough to
  be refuted, so both scientific groups are expected to score higher than
  doctrines whose proponents avoid tests. If the pseudoscientific group scores
  no lower, the items that read testability do not track it even coarsely.
- H2.3: the agreement of `appraise_amendment()` verdicts with individual
  experts is lower than the agreement of experts with each other. The test is
  framed so that it can count against claim C4: rejecting its null hypothesis
  means the rules agree with experts reliably less well than experts agree
  among themselves. C4 is supported if the lower limit of the difference lies
  above minus half the expert-expert kappa, that is, if any shortfall is
  reliably smaller than half of the experts' own agreement.

No directional hypothesis is made about corroborated against refuted theories.
The 0.8.0 documentation says that the score does not show that a theory is true,
and a better specified theory may be easier to refute as well as easier to
corroborate. The difference is estimated, and the two one-sided tests
procedure [@lakens2017] is applied with equivalence bounds of plus and minus
the SDD estimated in Study 1.

The secondary questions are these.

- How well does each item status agree with the experts' judgement of the
  corresponding item?
- Do items whose credit the package checks (against the graph, numeric bounds
  or the lexical screen) agree with experts better than items credited from a
  label or a filled field?
- Does the revised profile agree with experts better than the item statuses?
- How does the score correlate with expert-rated testability and with
  expert-rated empirical standing? The second correlation should be lower than
  the correlation with completeness if the score indexes specification rather
  than standing.
- Do the experts' testability ratings separate the known groups? This checks
  the classification.

## Design

Part A is a correlational validation study with known groups, in which every
theory of the shared sample is rated by `r nw(design$experts_per_theory)`
experts drawn from a pool of `r design$expert_pool`, assigned so that each
expert rates the same number of theories. Part B is an agreement study in which
each amendment episode is encoded by `r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` coders
and appraised by `r nw(design$experts_per_episode)` experts.

## Materials

Part A uses the segmented source passages of Study 1, with author names, theory
names and dates removed where the text allows. For each theory the experts
answer one question for each checklist item, phrased about the theory rather
than the file (@tbl-expert-items), with the answers 'yes', 'partly', 'no' and
'cannot tell'. They give three ratings from `r design$rating_scale[1]` to
`r design$rating_scale[2]`: how completely the theory is specified, how
testable it is as stated and how well supported it is by evidence. They also
say whether they knew the theory before.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-expert-items
#| tbl-cap: "Questions the experts answer about each theory, matched to the checklist items read from the repository."
questions <- c(
  falsifiability = "Does the passage state at least one prediction that rules out some possible result?",
  precision = "Does it state the size or the range of an expected value or effect?",
  risk_severity = "Do its predictions forbid a large part of the results that were possible before the study?",
  parsimony = "Does it add an assumption to protect a prediction that failed, without independent support for the assumption?",
  non_redundancy = "Are any two of its constructs defined so that they cannot be told apart?",
  construct_clarity = "Is each construct defined, with how it is measured and where it applies?",
  scope = "Does it state the conditions under which it applies?",
  logical_why = "Does each stated relation come with a reason or a mechanism?",
  causal_testability = "Does it state at least one causal relation?",
  diagnosticity = "Does it name a rival account and a result that would favour one over the other?",
  formalisation = "Is any part of it stated as a formal or computational model?",
  derivation_chain = "Do its predictions follow from its stated relations?")
stopifnot(length(setdiff(item_ids, names(questions))) == 0)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Item = item_ids, Question = unname(questions[item_ids])),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

Part B uses documented amendment episodes. An episode is eligible when a
published theory (the prior version) was revised in a later publication by
members of the same research programme (the amended version), when the later
publication states that the revision responds to at least one stated empirical
result, when that result is reported in a source published between the two
versions, and when both versions can be confined to passages that meet the
criteria of @sec-sample. Episodes are found by a search, fixed at registration,
for articles whose title or abstract presents a revised, extended or updated
version of a named theory in the behavioural sciences, and by a search for
published case studies that appraise an amendment in Lakatos's terms. Eligible
episodes are drawn at random. Experts receive the two passages and the report
of the result, with names and dates removed where possible, and a one-page
summary of the concepts of progressive and degenerating problemshifts written
from @lakatos1970 without reference to the package's rules. For each episode
they give a verdict (progressive, neutral or degenerating), their confidence
from `r design$confidence_scale[1]` to `r design$confidence_scale[2]`, the
reasons for the verdict and whether they recognise the episode.

The revised profile is the item-wise report in which each item's credit is
marked as checked by the package, declared by the author or not assessed, with
counts. Its definition will be fixed as code, registered with the analysis
scripts and applied to the files before any expert rating is unmasked.

## Participants and recruitment

Experts are researchers with a doctorate and publications either in the area of
the theories they rate or in research methods or the philosophy of science.
They are recruited through professional networks, the mailing lists of learned
societies and invitations to authors of methodological reviews, and receive an
honorarium. Experts do not take part as coders, classifiers or Study 3
participants, and none rates a theory or episode of which they are an author.
Amendment episodes are encoded by the Study 1 coders, under the same protocol
and the same assignment design, with each file recording the test outcomes that
the sources report as of the amended version.

## Procedure

Experts work online, alone and at their own pace. Each receives the passages
assigned to them in a random order, answers the item questions and the ratings
for each theory, and appraises the episodes assigned to them. They never see a
theory file, a package output, a group label or another expert's ratings. The
package's outputs are computed by the analyst from the coders' files and are
not joined to the expert data until the analysis scripts have been registered
and run on data with the group labels masked.

## Measures

- From the package, for each file: the checklist score, the status of each
  item and the revised profile.
- From the package, for each episode and coder: the verdict of
  `appraise_amendment()` on the coder's prior and amended files, with the other
  keys it reports.
- From the experts: the item answers, the three ratings and prior knowledge of
  each theory, and for each episode the verdict, confidence, reasons and
  recognition.
- From the classification panel: each theory's group.

## Analysis plan {#sec-s2-analysis}

For H2.1, the correlation between the theory-level mean score and the
theory-level mean completeness rating is estimated by Pearson's $r$ with a
Fisher $z$ interval, and by a bivariate mixed model with crossed random effects
for coders and experts as a check. Because the known groups widen the range of
theories, the correlation is also reported within the typical theories.

For H2.2, the theory-level mean scores of the pseudoscientific group are
compared with those of the corroborated and refuted groups by a one-sided
Welch test, and by a mixed model of the encodings with a fixed effect of group
and crossed random intercepts for theories and coders, whose group contrast is
reported with its interval.

For H2.3, Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960] is computed between the package's verdict
on each coder's encoding and each expert's verdict, and averaged over coders
and experts, and between each pair of experts, and averaged over pairs. The
difference between the two averages is the estimand. Its interval comes from a
bootstrap that resamples episodes, experts and coders. Linear weighted kappa,
with the verdicts ordered from degenerating to progressive, is reported as a
check. The agreement of the package's verdicts across the coders' encodings of
the same episode is reported separately, since it shows how much the verdict
depends on the encoding.

Item-level agreement between each item status (pass against any other status)
and the expert majority answer ('yes' against 'partly' or 'no') is reported by
kappa and Gwet's AC1 with bootstrap intervals over theories. 'Cannot tell' is
treated as missing for that item and, in a sensitivity analysis, as 'no'. A
theory with fewer than two expert ratings is left out of the analyses of
ratings, and the number left out is reported. The analyses assume that missing
ratings are missing at random given the theory and the expert.

## Sample size {#sec-s2-size}

For H2.2, the difference of interest is the smallest detectable difference of
the design scenario, `r f(sdd(sem_in[["content"]]), 1)` points: a smaller
average difference between groups would leave most individual theories of the
two groups indistinguishable by their scores. The within-group standard
deviation of a theory's mean score over its encodings is
$\sqrt{\sigma_t^2 + \mathrm{SEM}^2/m}$ with $m$ =
`r design$coders_per_theory`, and the noncentral $t$ distribution gives the
power of the one-sided comparison of one group with the other two taken
together.

```{r}
#| label: power-groups
power_groups <- function(n_g, delta, sd_w, alpha) {
  n1 <- n_g; n2 <- 2 * n_g; df <- n1 + n2 - 2
  ncp <- delta / sd_w / sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2)
  1 - pt(qt(1 - alpha / 2, df), df, ncp)
}
sd_within <- function(sd_t, sem) sqrt(sd_t^2 + sem^2 / design$coders_per_theory)
delta_mult <- c(`the SDD` = 1, `half the SDD` = 0.5)
grid_g <- expand.grid(n_g = design$ng_grid, sd_t = c("examples", "pooled"),
                      delta = names(delta_mult), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grid_g$delta_pts <- delta_mult[grid_g$delta] * sdd(sem_in[["content"]])
grid_g$power <- power_groups(grid_g$n_g, grid_g$delta_pts,
                             sd_within(sd_theory[grid_g$sd_t], sem_in[["content"]]),
                             design$alpha)
need_g <- aggregate(n_g ~ sd_t + delta,
                    data = grid_g[grid_g$power >= design$power, ], FUN = min)
n_group <- need_g$n_g[need_g$sd_t == "pooled" & need_g$delta == "the SDD"]
stopifnot(length(n_group) == 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-groups
#| tbl-cap: "Theories needed in each known group for the stated power in H2.2."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Theory SD` = paste0(need_g$sd_t, " (", f(sd_theory[need_g$sd_t]), ")"),
  Difference = paste0(need_g$delta, " (",
                      f(delta_mult[need_g$delta] * sdd(sem_in[["content"]]), 1),
                      " points)"),
  `Per group` = need_g$n_g, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

Under the widest spread of theories and a difference equal to the SDD,
`r n_group` theories per group give a power of at least `r pct(design$power)`.
The sample therefore needs at least `r length(known_groups) * n_group` theories
in the known groups and, so that the typical theories are not outnumbered by
any group, at least `r n_group` typical theories.

For H2.1, the correlation that can be observed is attenuated by the
unreliability of both measures. With the design scenario's ICC of
`r f(icc_mid)` for a single encoding, the mean of
`r nw(design$coders_per_theory)` encodings has a reliability of
`r f(sb(icc_mid, design$coders_per_theory))`. The reliability of the mean of
`r nw(design$experts_per_theory)` expert ratings is computed from an expert ICC
equal to the reviewer reliability and from a higher value of
`r f(design$expert_icc_alt)`. The power at the final sample size is given in
@sec-final-n.

```{r}
#| label: power-correlation
# Probability that the lower limit of the Fisher z interval exceeds rho0.
power_rho <- function(n, rho, rho0, alpha) {
  pnorm((atanh(rho) - atanh(rho0)) * sqrt(n - 3) - qnorm(1 - alpha / 2))
}
```

For H2.3, the agreement of `appraise_amendment()` with experts is simulated.
Each episode has a true verdict drawn with equal probabilities, which is an
assumption, since the distribution of verdicts among published amendments is
unknown. Each expert reproduces it with an accuracy that varies between experts
(standard deviation `r f(design$sd_expert_logit, 1)` on the logit scale) and
otherwise picks a verdict at random, and the package does the same for each
coder's encoding with its own accuracy. The expert accuracy is calibrated so
that the expected expert-expert kappa equals the reviewer kappa
(`r f(external$reviewer_kappa)`), `r f(design$expert_kappa_design)` or
`r f(design$expert_kappa_high)`, and the package's accuracy so that its
expected kappa with an expert equals the expert-expert kappa or falls short of
it by half.

```{r}
#| label: sim-episodes
kappa_fast <- function(a, b, ncat) {
  tab <- matrix(tabulate((a - 1) * ncat + b, ncat * ncat) / length(a), ncat,
                byrow = TRUE)
  po <- sum(diag(tab)); pe <- sum(rowSums(tab) * colSums(tab))
  (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
}
calibrate_mean_acc <- function(target_mean, sd) {
  uniroot(function(e) sum(GH$w * plogis(e + sd * GH$x)) - target_mean,
          c(-10, 10))$root
}
sim_episodes <- function(n_ep, kap_e, shortfall, reps) {
  share <- design$verdict_share; ncat <- length(share)
  mean_acc <- sqrt(kap_e)
  eta <- calibrate_mean_acc(mean_acc, design$sd_expert_logit)
  acc_p <- (kap_e - shortfall) / mean_acc
  n_exp <- design$experts_per_episode; n_enc <- design$coders_per_theory
  pr <- combn(n_exp, 2)
  est <- replicate(reps, {
    truth <- sample.int(ncat, n_ep, TRUE, share)
    rate <- function(a) ifelse(runif(n_ep) < a, truth,
                               sample.int(ncat, n_ep, TRUE, share))
    acc_e <- plogis(eta + rnorm(n_exp, 0, design$sd_expert_logit))
    E <- vapply(acc_e, rate, integer(n_ep))
    P <- vapply(rep(acc_p, n_enc), rate, integer(n_ep))
    k_ee <- mean(apply(pr, 2, function(p) kappa_fast(E[, p[1]], E[, p[2]], ncat)))
    k_pe <- mean(vapply(seq_len(n_enc), function(k)
      mean(vapply(seq_len(n_exp), function(e) kappa_fast(P[, k], E[, e], ncat), 0)),
      0))
    k_pe - k_ee
  })
  c(mean = mean(est), sd = sd(est))
}
set.seed(20261127)
kap_levels <- c(external$reviewer_kappa, design$expert_kappa_design,
                design$expert_kappa_high)
grid_e <- expand.grid(n_ep = design$ep_grid, kap_e = kap_levels,
                      shortfall = c("none", "half"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res_e <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_e)), function(i) {
  g <- grid_e[i, ]
  sim_episodes(g$n_ep, g$kap_e, if (g$shortfall == "half") g$kap_e / 2 else 0,
               design$reps_episode)
}, numeric(2)))
grid_e$mean <- res_e[, "mean"]
grid_e$sd <- res_e[, "sd"]
# Power to find the shortfall (upper interval limit below zero), treating the
# replication standard deviation as the standard error.
alt <- grid_e[grid_e$shortfall == "half", ]
alt$power <- pnorm(-alt$mean / alt$sd - z_crit)
alt$halfwidth_null <- z_crit * grid_e$sd[grid_e$shortfall == "none"]
ep_ok <- alt$n_ep[alt$kap_e == design$expert_kappa_design &
                    alt$power >= design$power]
n_episodes <- if (length(ep_ok)) min(ep_ok) else max(design$ep_grid)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-episodes
#| tbl-cap: "Amendment episodes: power to detect a package-expert agreement that falls short of expert-expert agreement by half, and the half-width of the interval for the difference when there is no shortfall."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Expert-expert kappa` = f(alt$kap_e), Episodes = alt$n_ep,
  Shortfall = f(alt$kap_e / 2), Power = f(alt$power),
  `Half-width, no shortfall` = f(alt$halfwidth_null), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

If experts agree with each other no better than journal reviewers do, no
feasible number of episodes can show that the package falls short of them, and
the study would instead show that expert appraisal of amendments is too
unreliable to serve as a criterion. With an expert-expert kappa of
`r f(design$expert_kappa_design)`, `r n_episodes` episodes give a power of at
least `r pct(design$power)` to detect a shortfall of half that value.

## Inference criteria

H2.1 is tested by the Fisher $z$ test of $\rho \le 0$, H2.2 by the one-sided
Welch test and H2.3 by the bootstrap interval for the
difference in kappa, each one-sided at level `r f(design$alpha / 2, 3)` with
the Holm procedure across the three. Claim C3 is supported if the lower limit of
the correlation exceeds `r f(design$rho_null)` and H2.2 is supported,
contradicted if the upper limit of the correlation lies below
`r f(design$rho_null)` or the pseudoscientific group's mean score is not below
the others', and otherwise open. Claim C4 is contradicted if H2.3 is
supported, supported if the lower limit of the difference lies above minus half
the expert-expert kappa, and otherwise open.

## Limitations

The criterion is expert judgement, which is itself fallible, and experts asked
to rate completeness may be swayed by what they know of a theory's standing.
Recording prior knowledge and the rating of empirical standing allows this to be
examined but not removed. Pseudoscientific doctrines are often well known, so
masking may fail, and their sources differ in genre from journal articles. The
known groups rest on the record available now, which may change. Part B gives
the experts a summary of Lakatos's concepts, so it tests whether the rules
reproduce what experts conclude with the same concepts, not whether the
concepts are the right ones. Encodings of episodes record outcomes as of the
amended version, while experts may know the later history of a well-known
episode, which the package does not read. Amendment episodes with both versions
in print may over-represent programmes that survived.

# Study 3: a randomised reader study {#sec-study3}

## Aims and hypotheses

Study 3 measures how often researchers and editors misread
`r nw(design$output_types)` outputs, the checklist score, the gate, the
dossier and the appraisal, and whether the wording of version 0.8.0 lowers that
rate relative to the wording of version 0.7.0. A misreading is endorsing a
statement about an output that the output does not support, for example that a
theory with a higher checklist score is more likely to be true, that a passing
gate shows that the predictions have been tested, that the dossier's test
outcomes were verified by the package or that a progressive verdict shows the
amendment predicted facts not used in building it. Automation bias, the
tendency to over-rely on automation [@goddard2012], occurs in naive and expert
users alike and is not prevented by training or instructions
[@parasuraman2010], while design factors such as where advice appears on the
screen are among the reported mitigators [@goddard2012]. The wording of a
display is therefore a plausible lever and an uncertain one.

- H3.1: the probability of endorsing a misreading is lower in the 0.8.0 wording
  than in the 0.7.0 wording.
- H3.2: in the 0.8.0 wording, the rate at which participants endorse the
  statements that read the score as a judgement of truth is below
  `r pct(design$truth_tolerance)`, a tolerance that is our value judgement.
- H3.3: the 0.8.0 wording does not lower the odds of endorsing correct readings
  by more than an odds ratio of `r f(design$ni_margin_or)`, so that a lower
  misreading rate is not bought by making readers reject everything.
